content.thinking: I need to fix the citation to reference AL1 instead of A1, cite only F1, and remove the specific time references. For the action items, I should number mine as AI-3, AI-4, AI-5 since AI-1 and AI-2 already exist, matching them to the correct contributing factors.

action_items.item: Add an alert on sustained heap growth, such as a rising trend in heap against the container limit, so a slow climb pages well before it nears the limit.
Add a soak or load test that records many distinct shoppers and asserts that process memory and the size of in-process stores stay bounded. Run it before release.

Capture a heap profile or object-count snapshot from a replica during a climb, to confirm that the last-seen shopper store is what holds the memory. Do this before or alongside merging the fix, and check that memory stays flat after it ships.

causal_chain.step: Memory use of io-shop climbed against its container limit and paged. The series averaged {series_while_broken} over the incident and reached {series_at_worst} at its worst, against {series_before} before. The heap warnings showed it rising from {G9c6f.5} to {G9c6f.6} against a {G9c6f.1} limit. Failed requests did not measurably rise: {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before, peaking at {errors_at_worst}, which is within normal variation. The harm was memory pressure on the service that renders account pages, not a measured rise in failures.
The io-shop process heap grew steadily from the onset and was not released. The heap warnings were logged in every minute they covered, and the highest value came at the end.

Nothing external set it off. No production change was read in the day before the onset, and the flag provider showed no recent flag changes. The ClientDisconnected errors and the account-page error-rate warnings began before the onset and match their usual levels, so they are baseline noise and not the cause.

The likely reason the heap is never released is an unbounded in-process store. By Code-Fix's static reading, `_LAST_SEEN` gains an entry for every shopper rendered and has no eviction except a full reset. This reading was not run or verified, so it is unconfirmed. If correct, a steady stream of new shoppers would grow memory even with flat traffic, matching the climb Code-Fix put at about {F1.1} to {F1.2}.

Restarting io-shop cleared the condition and the paging rule stopped firing. That fits state held inside the process, but it only resets the climb. The record does not show which data structure held the memory, so the chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The restart only resets the climb. Until the bounded-store fix is merged and deployed, memory will climb again after any restart.

The page came only after the rule's wait of {rule_waits} with the condition holding. Heap warnings were already being logged earlier, but no alert on the heap's growth trend was seen, so a steady climb was caught only when it was far along.
No test or pre-release check was seen that exercises many distinct shoppers and watches memory stay bounded, so an unbounded in-process store could ship without being noticed.
The leak mechanism rests on a static code reading that nothing ran. The record has no heap profile showing what held the memory.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, starting at {began}, the memory use of the shop service climbed steadily toward its container limit. Failed requests stayed within their normal range, so the measured harm was the memory climb. Left alone, it would have put account pages at risk of slowing or failing. Argus found no deploy or flag change that could explain it, and it restarted the service. Memory returned to normal and the alert stopped firing. A code reading suggests an in-process store of shoppers that grows without limit. A draft fix has been proposed and is awaiting review. Until it ships, the climb is expected to return after any restart.

got_lucky: Failed requests stayed within normal variation, so shoppers were not measurably affected before the restart. A longer climb could have reached the memory limit.
went_well: Argus read metrics, changes, logs and flag history, ruled out a deploy or flag trigger, and restarted the service. The restart was confirmed soon after it was made.
Code-Fix proposed a bounded, least-recently-used fix with tests, ready for review.
went_wrong: The restart treats only the symptom. The climb will return until the fix ships.
The leak mechanism is unverified. It rests on a code reading and no heap profile was seen.
Latency degradation is not shown in the measured record, so its impact on shoppers was not measured.

input.root_cause: Memory in the running io-shop process grew without being released from about the onset. Code-Fix's reading of the source, which nothing ran and which is unverified, points to a module-level dictionary of last-seen shoppers, `io_shop.visits._LAST_SEEN`. It gains an entry for every new shopper and has no eviction short of a full reset, so the heap fills steadily under flat traffic. The record shows only that memory climbed and that a restart cleared it. It does not show which structure held the memory.
input.symptom: Shop service memory climbed toward its limit, putting account pages at risk
